notes.body: Earlier the chapter was careful with its arithmetic: Kun is two letters, fa-yakun is five, 'seven letters in all,' and from those seven letters seven things branch. Then it returns to the same formula — 'a will, a command, by a saying' — and says this 'comes to twelve letters,' and builds the twelve constellations on it. So the same three-word saying is counted as seven letters in one place and twelve in another, and nothing tells me which count governs what, or why the number changed when the words did not. Are the seven and the twelve two different tallies of the same phrase, or of different phrases? I could not resolve it from the chapter, and the whole scheme of signs hangs on the number.

The twelve constellations are given 'witnesses,' and the witnesses are 'seven kingdoms'; then the twelve earthly islands get 'seventeen seas' as their witnesses. These two numbers simply arrive. Nothing earlier prepared me for seven kingdoms or seventeen seas, and nothing after explains what a 'witness' to a constellation or an island is, or why the count is seven in the sky and seventeen on the earth when the signs themselves are twelve in both. Every other number in the passage was derived from something — the letters, the words — but these two are asserted flat. A first-time reader is left holding two figures with nothing behind them.
